opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting paper, and an important one, because it pushes on a question I care a lot about: can these systems tell us when they're likely to be wrong? The core finding, as I read it, is that if you ask a large model to evaluate its own proposed answer, essentially "is this answer true?", the probability it assigns is reasonably well calibrated, especially for the bigger models and when the question is formatted carefully, say multiple choice with the options visible. They also trained the model to predict P(IK), the probability that "I know" the answer before generating it, and that worked to a degree as well.

That said, I'd be cautious about the headline. The "mostly" in the title is doing a lot of work. Calibration held up best in-distribution, and it degraded when they moved to new tasks or changed the format. That's exactly the setting where we most need uncertainty estimates. If I'm deploying a system in the open world, the dangerous cases are the novel ones, the inputs unlike anything in training, and that's where self-assessment seems to be weakest.

I also think we should be careful with the anthropomorphic language. Saying the model "knows what it knows" suggests some kind of introspective access, a metacognitive faculty. What they've really shown is that there's a signal in the model's internal representations that correlates with correctness and can be read out or trained. That's useful, but it's a statistical property of the network, not self-knowledge in any rich sense. It's closer to what we've studied for years in classifier confidence and selective prediction, where a model abstains when its confidence is low.

And that connects to my broader view. I've argued that we need systems with competence models, models of their own competence, so they can say "I don't know" or hand off to a human. Large language models are trained to produce fluent continuations, not to represent epistemic uncertainty, and they don't distinguish knowledge from plausibility. So results like this are encouraging evidence that the raw material for uncertainty is in there, but I don't think you get reliable uncertainty for free. You need explicit mechanisms, such as calibration on held-out data, conformal methods that give guarantees, retrieval so claims can be checked against sources, and continued evaluation under distribution shift.

So my summary would be: a valuable step, a real and useful signal, but not a solution to hallucination or to trustworthy deployment. We still need to engineer the system around the model so it knows, in a verifiable way, when it shouldn't be trusted.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's an important paper, and I want to give the Anthropic team credit for asking the right question, which is: can a model assess the reliability of its own outputs? That's been a central concern of mine for a long time. In my view, a competent AI system needs to know what it knows and what it doesn't know, and most of the systems we've been deploying don't have that property.

What Kadavath and colleagues showed is that if you ask a large language model, "Is this answer you just gave correct, true or false?" the probability it assigns to "true" is reasonably well calibrated, at least on the kinds of benchmarks they tested, and that calibration improves with scale. They also looked at this notion of P(IK), the probability that the model knows the answer, before it actually produces one, and found that it generalizes somewhat across tasks. So that's encouraging. It suggests that there is some internal signal that correlates with correctness.

But I'd put the emphasis on the "mostly" in the title, and I have several concerns. The first is that calibration was measured on multiple-choice and short-answer tasks, in distribution, where the model has seen enormous amounts of related data. The hard cases for any machine learning system are the out-of-distribution cases, the novel situations, and that's exactly where I'd expect self-assessment to break down. They did see degradation when they changed the format or moved to different tasks, and that's the signal I pay attention to. Calibration is not a property of the model alone; it's a property of the model together with the distribution of questions it's being asked.

The second concern is that "knowing what you know" in the paper is a statistical statement about an ensemble of questions. It doesn't mean the model has an epistemic state about any particular question. From a safety and engineering standpoint, what we actually want is a per-instance guarantee, or at least a reliable per-instance flag that says, "I shouldn't be trusted here." Aggregate calibration is necessary but not sufficient for that.

Third, there's a brittleness issue. Later work found that these self-evaluations can be quite sensitive to prompting and that models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback can become less calibrated, because the training pushes them toward confident, agreeable outputs. So the property is fragile under exactly the kind of fine-tuning that's done before deployment.

And finally, I'd note that we have a broader literature on this, open category detection, anomaly detection, conformal prediction, and I'd like to see those tools brought to bear. Conformal methods, for instance, can give you distribution-free coverage guarantees that don't rely on trusting the model's introspection.

So my overall take is: it's a promising result, it's evidence that the information is in there somewhere, but I would not build a safety case on a language model's self-report of its own competence. That has to be verified from the outside.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an encouraging result, but we need to be careful about what we mean by “know.” There’s a difference between a model assigning confidence to an answer and reliably recognizing when it’s outside the conditions under which that confidence is meaningful.

The interesting question is whether the model can distinguish its correct answers from its incorrect ones. If it can, that gives us something useful: perhaps a way to abstain, ask for more information, or refer a question to a person. But we also need to ask whether that ability holds up when the questions change. A confidence estimate that works on one distribution may be misleading on another.

So I’d take the findings as evidence that there’s a useful signal to investigate, rather than as a demonstration that the uncertainty problem is solved. For deployment, what matters is whether we can turn that signal into a dependable decision about when to trust an answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting distinction is between a model having information about whether its answer is correct and being able to use that information reliably. Those aren’t quite the same thing. A model might give you a useful confidence estimate under one set of conditions, but we still need to ask whether that estimate holds up when the questions change or when the model encounters something outside its experience.

So I would take the findings as encouraging evidence that there’s something there to work with, rather than as a solution to the problem of knowing when to trust these systems. The practical question is whether we can use that signal to get a model to say, “I don’t know,” or to seek additional evidence, at the right times. And that requires evaluating the errors it makes when it’s confident, not just how well confidence tracks accuracy on average.
